summary.text: A lava flow is an outpouring of molten lava during an effusive eruption, unlike the ash and fragments an explosive eruption throws out.
Lava usually erupts at 800 to 1,200 °C and is about as thick as ketchup, yet it can travel far because a solid crust forms and insulates the liquid inside.
Silica controls how runny lava is: silica-rich felsic lava is extremely viscous, while less viscous basalt can flow long distances and build low-profile shield volcanoes.

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Italian, first for a stream after sudden rain

items.prompt: Lava meets cool air the moment it leaves a vent. How can a flow still keep moving for long distances before it freezes?

options.label: It heats itself up as it runs downhill
A crust forms that keeps the inside hot
The air above it traps the volcano's heat
It stays thinner than water the whole way

items.explain: Exposed lava quickly grows a solid crust that insulates the liquid inside, keeping it hot and fluid enough to flow.

items.prompt: Two lavas erupt at the same temperature, one with 70% silica and one with 48%. Which is likelier to run a long way from the vent?

options.label: The 70% one, because silica makes it slippery
Neither, since silica only changes the colour
The 70% one, because it holds more gas
The 48% one, because it is less viscous

items.explain: Silica makes lava polymerize and thicken, so low-silica basalt is far runnier and can flow long distances.

items.prompt: About how thick is most molten lava as it flows?

options.label: About as runny as water
About as runny as cooking oil
About as thick as ketchup
About as stiff as window glass

items.explain: Most molten lava has roughly the viscosity of ketchup, some 10,000 to 100,000 times that of water.

items.prompt: Very sticky, silica-rich rhyolite magma rises toward the surface. How does it usually erupt?

options.label: Explosively, leaving broken fragments
As long, fast rivers of lava
As a calm, glowing lava lake
As a thin sheet across the plain

items.explain: Because felsic lava is so viscous, it usually erupts explosively and produces pyroclastic, or fragmental, deposits.

items.prompt: Basalt lava erupts on the sea floor instead of on land. What does it typically form?

options.label: Rounded pillow lavas
Tall lava domes
Columns of pumice
Thick block lavas

items.explain: Underwater, basaltic lavas can form pillow lavas, which resemble some pahoehoe lavas on land.

items.prompt: A hardened basalt flow is 10 m thick, yet at any one moment the moving lava was much thinner. How can that be?

options.label: The rock swelled like ice as it cooled
Ash fell on it and added the extra height
Fresh lava kept pushing up its solid crust
Rainwater soaked in and made the rock swell

items.explain: Basaltic flows can inflate as a continued supply of lava presses on the solidified crust and lifts it.
